Societe Nationale de I Electricite & Du Gaz SpA Insolvency Sends Shockwaves Through Algeria’s Energy Sector

Algiers—The ongoing insolvency proceedings at Societe Nationale de I Electricite & Du Gaz SpA, one of Algeria’s prominent oil and gas producers, have begun to disrupt the company’s day-to-day operations and cast uncertainty over the region’s energy landscape.

The company, a key employer in the Oran and Hassi Messaoud regions, initiated proceedings last week after reporting sustained financial losses and an inability to meet mounting debt obligations. As the situation unfolds, Societe Nationale de I Electricite & Du Gaz SpA’s management has confirmed that several projects have been suspended and routine maintenance at some production facilities has been delayed.

“We are doing everything we can to maintain essential services, but there are significant constraints on our operations,” said interim spokesperson Ahmed Lounis. “Our immediate priority is the safety of our workers and the stability of our core infrastructure.”

Industry analysts warn that the insolvency could have ripple effects for both the local economy and Algeria’s broader energy sector. “Societe Nationale de I Electricite & Du Gaz SpA is not just another producer—it is a crucial link in the national energy supply chain,” said Salima Chergui, an energy analyst based in Algiers. “Production slowdowns may impact both domestic supply and export commitments if the situation is not resolved swiftly.”

Trade unions have voiced concern for the workforce, with the National Energy Workers’ Union estimating that over 2,000 jobs may be at risk if restructuring or liquidation occurs. “There is deep anxiety among employees and their families,” said union representative Mohamed Khelil. “We urge all stakeholders to prioritize workers’ livelihoods during this difficult period.”

As of Monday, court-appointed administrators are assessing the company’s assets and liabilities. The process is expected to continue over the coming weeks, with further impacts on operations likely as decisions about the company’s future are made. Local suppliers and contractors, including the Tizi Ouzou-based Atlas Services, are already reporting delays in payments.
